topics.topic: the unit 2 vocabulary and question list (book pp. 41-42) - ism/ismii, the possessive suffixes -ii/-ka/-ki, maa vs shuu for 'what', ayna/wayn for 'where', min, the question particle hal, anaa/anta/anti, naam and laa, madiina, ahlan and its replies ahlan bika/biki, and the formal haDratuka/haDratuki - taught throughout in both Fusha and Shami variants

connecting letters into words - the two-step method (first hear which letters are in the word, then decide which of the four forms each takes based on whether the PREVIOUS letter connects leftward), worked on baab and then through the unit 2 drill 2 dictation words with students called to the board

waaw, the day's new letter and the first vowel after alif - independent and connecting shapes only (it connects to the right alone), her habit of darkening the loop so it cannot be mistaken for meem, its dual life as vowel and consonant, and the words tuut, thawb, thawaab and tuubuu built from it

taa and thaa - identical to baa in skeleton, distinguished only by dot position and count (two dots above, three dots above), the handwriting alternatives of a dash and a caret, all four positional forms of each, and the rule that the tooth stays straight and always shorter than the alif

announcements.text: TWO homeworks are due this week, which she flagged deliberately: Homework 1 is due Wednesday 9/2 and Homework 2 is due Friday 9/4. Homework 1 is entirely on Lingco (unit 2 drills 1 and 3) with nothing to submit to Canvas. Homework 2 is mostly written dictation - done on paper, photographed, uploaded to Canvas.

Every written homework needs a four-part heading: name, homework number, drill number, lesson number. She said 'I need to see those four things' and repeated it as a standing requirement, not a one-off.
iPhone and Mac photos must NOT be uploaded as HEIC - Canvas cannot read that format. Directly relevant since the dictation homework is submitted as photographs.
Lingco work must reach 100%. She allows 100 attempts, so it is a keep-trying-until-correct system rather than a graded-once one.

The Canvas green module checkmark will NOT appear for Lingco-only weeks, because there is nothing to submit on the Canvas side. She said students who want the checkmark can screenshot Lingco and upload that, and that she would prefer it since it saves her checking two places - but it is optional and she checks Lingco regardless.

She will NOT correct the dictation drills after submission - they get corrected in class, with students called to the board. From drill 3 onward the class writes on the board rather than watching her do it, so arriving without having attempted the drills means being stuck at the board.

Final exam signal on the greeting vocabulary: she is not requiring the class to READ or WRITE these words yet, because the letters have not all been taught, but by the end of the course they must be able to do both. She used haDratuka as her example of a word that could appear on the final in Arabic script.

Final exam signal on translation method: start word-for-word, then make the result read naturally in the target language. 'On the final exam, when you translate, start word for word, but then make it make sense in English, not literal translation.'
Vocabulary that is REQUIRED versus optional: baab (door) and tuut (berries) are required additions to the vocab list. taab (he repented) she offered as optional extra credit for anyone who wants it.

assigned_reading.note: the unit 2 greeting and question-word vocabulary list; she said it can be followed from the book or from her slides. These are PRINTED page labels as she spoke them, not physical PDF pages. No due date was attached to the reading itself.

off_slide: Opened the class in prayer, thanking God for the second week and for students enthusiastic about Arabic, and asking that they process, memorise and start USING the language

Regional handwriting digression: Tunisia teaches children to avoid the fast style and write close to the printed script, while Syria, Jordan, Lebanon and Egypt write quickly and squiggly, keeping the pen down and adding all the dots and carets at the end. She left two-dots versus a dash entirely to student preference, noting she herself never thinks in dots - she goes straight to the dash unconsciously
Reassured a student struggling with the rolled R by telling them about a student who nearly quit over that sound and now 'we cannot stop her from rolling'

Separated the letter from the letter's NAME: baa, taa and thaa are spelled with a hamza, the glottal stop, and she warned the class not to confuse hamza with Hamza the personal name, which has an H sound

The height rule, given as a drawing warning rather than a fact: the tooth must always be visibly shorter than the alif, never the same height, and a group of letters yet to come sits between the two in height. She also warned that a curved tooth stops being baa/taa/thaa and becomes nuun

Her personal habit of darkening the middle of the waaw loop, which the printed script does not do, purely so a fast-written waaw cannot be misread as meem. Explicitly flagged as her preference, not a rule

Answered Parker's question about whether the waaw loop sits above the line: she writes the whole letter above the line, the book puts the loop above and dips below, and neither is wrong - though the book's version makes more sense on lined paper, and when waaw connects it has to dip

Told the class to play with Arabic fonts in a Word document to get their eyes used to different typefaces, and pointed at a calligrapher on Lingco worth watching, noting calligraphy is a serious specialism in the Arab world

Taught each vocabulary word with more than its gloss: taab is 'he repented' and nothing to do with English 'tab', baat is 'he slept over somewhere', tuut is berries in formal Arabic but also the noise a train makes for Arabic children, and thawb is the white garment Saudi men wear, closer to a jacket in Egypt, and can also be a woman's dress

When a student asked why tuubuu ends the way it does, she explained the plural verb suffix, then warned that Arabic plurals are 'very inconsistent' and that broken plurals - possibly inherited from Syriac - are coming in a later unit

Taught haDratuka/haDratuki with its literal sense of 'your presence' and the cultural context that Egyptians use titles and formal address heavily, partly to make people feel important, and that it is the right register for professors, bosses, strangers and older people

Taught Fusha and Shami side by side throughout rather than picking one - maa against shuu, ayna against wayn, anta against inte, ahlan bika against ahlan fiiki - and told the class to use whichever is easier for them, so they are not thrown when they meet a different dialect
Word-order point made through a live translation: Arabic asks 'from where are you', and the class had to reorder it into natural English
Switched into student view on screen and walked through both Lingco drills when a student said they were not seeing what she was seeing

notes: HOMEWORK 1 IS DUE TODAY (Wednesday 9/2) on Lingco. This transcript was stranded in the capture pipeline and only reached the inbox on 9/2, so this deadline had no chance to appear in any earlier brief. It is the most urgent item across the whole distill run.

Three NEW letters were taught today: taa, thaa and waaw. Combined with alif and baa from the previous week, the taught set is now alif, baa, taa, thaa, waaw. This is the gate for the Arabic Anki deck, which has been held to alif and baa since 8/28 - it can now open to five letters.

nuun, meem and yaa were each named, but ONLY as contrasts - nuun as what a curved tooth accidentally becomes, meem as what a fast waaw can be mistaken for, yaa as a letter coming later. None of them was taught, and none should enter the deck.

Vocabulary is explicitly split into required and optional: baab and tuut required, taab offered as optional extra. The pp. 41-42 greeting list she taught in full and expects spoken on Thursday. thawb, baat, thawaab and tuubuu came out of drills and examples rather than the vocab list, so their status is unstated.
The page numbers 41-42 are PRINTED labels as she spoke them, not physical PDF pages. Anything matching this against the Alif Baa PDF needs the printed-to-physical offset, not a raw page index.

One genuine ambiguity worth checking on Lingco rather than trusting this record: early in class she said 'there is a drill 2 on your book, it is part of your homework one', but at the end she said Homework 1 is drills 1 and 3, both on Lingco. A student asked where drill 2 went and her answer was hedged ('This is probably drill 2, week two'). Drill 2 was worked through together in class. The commitment above uses her FINAL statement.

Reading and writing these greeting words is not required yet - she said so directly, because the letters are not all taught. But she named haDratuka as the kind of word that could appear in Arabic script on the final, so the writing requirement arrives before the course ends.
Parker was active in this class - he asked the question about where the waaw loop sits relative to the line, and answered a vocabulary question correctly. Both are audible in the recording.

Transcript quality is poor on exactly the material that matters, because Teams has no Arabic. Letter names came through as: alif = 'LF', 'Eleph', 'left', 'alive'; baa = 'bar', 'Bob', 'va'; taa = 'tab', 'tub', 'town'; thaa = 'cell', 'that'; waaw = 'wall', 'wow', 'well'. Also 'hands up' and 'Global stuff' for hamza and glottal stop, 'carrots' for carets, 'Lingo'/'Lango'/'Vingo' for Lingco, 'Chami'/'Siami' for Shami, 'Fos Ha' for Fusha, 'Smokey'/'smug'/'smack' for ismuki/ismuka, 'Nam' for naam, 'hen'/'hell' for hal, and 'Medinet' for madiinat.

No Arabic script is recorded anywhere in this file. The transcript contains none, and reconstructing spellings from mangled transliteration would put wrong orthography into the vocabulary lane - the letters and words above are transliteration only, to be checked against her slides or the book before any card is made.
